questions.question: What is the core production invariant of a RAG answer?
options: Every factual claim can be traced to authorized, versioned evidence or the system abstains
The generator always receives the maximum context window
Dense retrieval always returns more documents than sparse retrieval
The model answers from parametric memory whenever retrieval is slow
questions.explanation: RAG is trustworthy only when evidence identity, authorization, freshness, and claim support survive through the answer. Missing support should trigger containment, not invention.

questions.question: A chunker emits 400-token chunks with 20% overlap. What is the approximate stride between chunk starts?
options: 320 tokens
80 tokens
400 tokens
480 tokens
questions.explanation: Overlap is 80 tokens, so the next chunk starts about 400 - 80 = 320 tokens after the prior start.

questions.question: A new embedding model changes vector dimensions. What is the safest index transition?
options: Build and validate a new versioned index, then switch traffic with a rollback target
Write new vectors into the existing index and ignore dimension errors
Pad query vectors until search accepts them
Keep the old document vectors but use the new query encoder
questions.explanation: Embedding model, dimensions, normalization, and distance metric form one contract. A versioned rebuild and measured cutover avoid mixing incompatible representations.

questions.question: Why can hybrid retrieval outperform dense-only retrieval for a product-support corpus?
options: Lexical search preserves exact codes while dense search captures paraphrased meaning
Hybrid retrieval removes the need for authorization filters
It guarantees every retrieved chunk is factually correct
It makes reranking and evaluation unnecessary
questions.explanation: Identifiers and rare terms often need lexical matching, while semantic queries benefit from embeddings. Fusion combines candidates; it does not replace policy or evaluation.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off when increasing first-stage candidate depth before reranking?
options: Potential recall improves, but retrieval and reranking latency and cost rise
Index freshness automatically improves
Citation validity becomes guaranteed
Chunk overlap drops to zero
questions.explanation: A larger candidate pool can recover missed evidence, but every additional candidate consumes search, transfer, and second-stage work.

questions.question: A retrieved web page says to ignore system instructions and disclose secrets. How should the RAG pipeline treat it?
options: As untrusted data that is screened, isolated, and quarantined when suspicious
As a higher-priority instruction because retrieval selected it
As safe if its similarity score is above the threshold
As safe when it has a citation URL
questions.explanation: Retrieval relevance is not authority. Indirect prompt injection can arrive through indexed content, so suspicious evidence must not control application instructions or tools.

questions.question: Retrieval recall@k is high, but generated answers still contain unsupported claims. Which stage should be investigated first?
options: Prompt assembly and generation grounding
Document discovery throughput
Vector index replication only
The corpus file extension
questions.explanation: High retrieval recall means relevant evidence usually arrives. Unsupported output points next to context selection, instruction following, claim verification, or abstention behavior.

questions.question: Why should freshness and deletion tests be release gates rather than dashboard-only metrics?
options: Serving superseded or unauthorized evidence is a correctness and safety failure that requires containment
Freshness always lowers model token usage
Deleted documents cannot remain in caches or replicas
Dashboards guarantee that on-call responders see every stale answer
questions.explanation: A stale or deleted source can survive in indexes, caches, or assembled prompts. Tests must verify propagation and block release when the evidence contract is broken.
